items.title: Unit 3, Ask Questions (open-ended): A photo shows a crash-test dummy wearing a bicycle helmet being dropped onto a steel anvil, with a high-speed camera recording. Write questions you could add to a class question board.

body.html: A photo of a helmet drop test. There is no single numerical answer; you are asked to write good, testable questions.
The helmet stops the dummy's head quickly, so forces, momentum and energy are all involved. Good questions can be answered by measuring mass, speed, time or force.

Sample questions you could post: How fast is the head moving just before it hits? How much force acts on the head during the stop? Why does foam inside a helmet reduce injury? Where does the head's kinetic energy go when the foam crushes?

answer.html: "How does crushing foam change the force on the head?", "How does the stopping time depend on the thickness of the foam?", "Where does the kinetic energy of the falling head go?"

check.html: Each question can be tested with a measurement (drop height, stopping time, force sensor reading).

items.title: Module 9, CER (claim, evidence, reasoning): How can a spacecraft drifting through space change its direction using small thrusters?

body.html: Make a claim about how a spacecraft with nothing to push against can start moving in a new direction, then support it.
A spacecraft and its gas form a closed, isolated system. Total momentum is constant, so when thruster gas is expelled one way, the spacecraft gains equal momentum the other way (Newton's third law).

Claim: A thruster pushes gas out in one direction, and the gas pushes the spacecraft the opposite way. Evidence: In recoil situations (a skater pushing off a partner, a gun and bullet, carts pushed apart by a spring) the two parts end with equal and opposite momentum: 𝑚<sub>craft</sub>𝑣<sub>craft</sub> = −𝑚<sub>gas</sub>𝑣<sub>gas</sub>. Reasoning: With no outside force, the total momentum stays the same. The gas has momentum one way, so the craft must have equal momentum the other way. No air or ground is needed.

answer.html: A spacecraft turns or speeds up by recoil: firing thruster gas in one direction gives the craft an equal momentum in the opposite direction, by conservation of momentum.

check.html: The momenta of gas and craft add to zero, matching what a spring-loaded cart pair does.

items.title: Focus Question: How do bicycle helmets protect riders in a crash?

body.html: The impulse needed to stop a head, 𝐹𝛥𝑡= 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝑝<sub>𝑖</sub>, is fixed by the head's mass and speed. Crushable foam lengthens 𝛥𝑡, so the average force 𝐹 is smaller. The shell also spreads the force over a bigger area.

answer.html: The foam crushes slowly, increasing the stopping time. The same change in momentum then needs a smaller average force, spread over a larger area, so injury is less likely.

check.html: Same 𝛥𝑝 with a larger 𝛥𝑡 means a smaller 𝐹.

items.title: Figure 1 prompt: A 0.43-kg soccer ball is kicked. The force from the foot rises steadily from 0 to 1200 N in 5.0 ms, then falls steadily back to 0 in the next 5.0 ms (a triangle- shaped force-time graph). How can you calculate the change in the ball's velocity, and what is it if the ball starts at rest?

body.html: 𝑚= 0.43 kg, peak force 1200 N, total contact time 10.0 ms, triangle shape, 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= 0. Find 𝛥𝑣.
The impulse equals the area under the force-time graph, and impulse equals the change in momentum: 𝐽= 𝑚𝛥𝑣.
The area of a triangle is one half base times height.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑣=<sub> </sub><sup>area</sup><sup> </sup><sup>under</sup><sup> </sup><sup>the</sup><sup> </sup><sup>𝐹</sup><sup>–</sup><sup>𝑡</sup><sup> </sup><sup>graph</sup>
. Here the impulse is 6.0 N · s and the ball leaves at 14 m/s in the direction of the force.

check.html: Average force is half the peak, 600 N, for 0.010 s gives 6.0 N·s. Same.

items.title: Figure 5, Analyze: A gymnast does a flip with her body tucked into a tight ball, then straightens her body into a layout just before landing. How does straightening out affect her rotation?

body.html: In the air, gravity gives no torque about her center of mass, so 𝐿= 𝐼𝜔 stays constant. Straightening moves mass away from the rotation axis, which increases 𝐼.
𝐼<sub>𝑖</sub>𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>= 𝐼<sub>𝑓</sub>𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub>, so 𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>(𝐼<sub>𝑖</sub>/ 𝐼<sub>𝑓</sub>). A larger 𝐼<sub>𝑓</sub> gives a smaller 𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub>.

answer.html: Straightening out increases her moment of inertia, so she rotates more slowly. That slows her flip so she can see the floor and land.

check.html: Tucking does the opposite: smaller 𝐼, faster spin.

items.title: Cause and Effect (Crosscutting Concepts): A student sits on a rotating stool holding a dumbbell in each outstretched hand. A partner gives the stool a push to start it spinning. What causes the spin to start, and how could you test what happens when she pulls the dumbbells in?

body.html: The partner's push applies a torque for a short time. This angular impulse changes the angular momentum: 𝜏𝛥𝑡= 𝛥𝐿. After the push, the bearing has almost no friction, so 𝐿= 𝐼𝜔 is nearly constant. Pulling the weights in lowers 𝐼, so 𝜔 increases. Work (test plan): Start the stool spinning with the weights out. Video the spin and count rotations per second. Pull the weights in and count again. Repeat with heavier weights. Compare 𝐼<sub>out</sub>𝜔<sub>out</sub> with 𝐼<sub>in</sub>𝜔<sub>in</sub> using estimated values of 𝐼.

answer.html: Cause: the partner's push gives a torque and an angular impulse that starts the spin. Effect: with no outside torque, pulling the weights in lowers 𝐼 and raises 𝜔 so that 𝐼𝜔 stays constant. Test by measuring the spin rate with the weights out and in.

check.html: 𝜔<sub>in</sub> / 𝜔<sub>out</sub> should equal 𝐼<sub>out</sub> / 𝐼<sub>in</sub>.

items.title: 1 (Lesson 1 Practice, parts a–b): A 1450-kg pickup truck moves at 88 km/h west. (a) Find its momentum and sketch it. (b) A 3200-kg delivery truck has the same momentum. What is its velocity?

body.html: 𝑚<sub>1</sub> = 1450 kg, 𝑣<sub>1</sub> = 88 km/h = 24.4 m/s west; 𝑚<sup>2</sup> = 3200 kg, 𝑝<sub>2</sub> = 𝑝<sub>1</sub>. Find 𝑝<sub>1</sub> and 𝑣<sup>2</sup>.
Momentum is 𝑝= 𝑚𝑣, a vector in the same direction as the velocity.
Convert speed: 88 km/h ×<sub> </sub><sup>1000</sup><sup> </sup><sup>m</sup>
Sketch: a truck with an arrow pointing west (to the left) above it labeled 𝑝<sub>1</sub>; the axis +x points west. For the heavier truck 𝑝<sub>2</sub> = 𝑝<sub>1</sub>, so

answer.html: 3.54 × 10<sup>4</sup> kg · m/s, west.
11.1 m/s (about 40 km/h), west.

check.html: The delivery truck has about 2.2 times the mass, so its speed is about 1/2.2 of 24.4 m/s, or 11.1 m/s.

items.title: 2 (Lesson 1 Practice): A 1240-kg van travels north at 72.0 km/h. The driver brakes for 3.5 s with an average braking force of 3.6 × 103 N. (a) What is the impulse on the van? (b) What are the van's final momentum and velocity?

body.html: 𝑚= 1240 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= 72.0 km/h = + 20.0 m/s (north positive), 𝛥𝑡= 3.5 s, 𝐹= −3.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> N (braking force points south). Find 𝐹𝛥𝑡, 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>, 𝑣<sup>𝑓</sup>.
Impulse-momentum theorem 𝐹𝛥𝑡= 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝑝<sub>𝑖</sub>.
Sketch: "before" van with a long arrow north labeled 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= 20.0 m/s, "after" van with a shorter arrow north labeled 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>= 9.8 m/s, and a south-pointing arrow for the impulse.

answer.html: 1.3 × 10<sup>4</sup> N · s (1.3 × 10<sup>4</sup> kg · m/s), directed south.
𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>= 1.2 × 10<sup>4</sup> kg · m/s north; 𝑣<sup>𝑓</sup>= 9.8 m/s north (about 35 km/h).

check.html: The van slows but still moves north; 9.8 m/s is less than 20.0 m/s.

items.title: 3 (Lesson 1 Practice): A 5.5-kg cart rolls along a track at 1.5 m/s. It receives two impulses in a row, both along its line of motion. First, a push of +12 N acts for 1.5 s (in the direction of motion). Then a push of −15 N (opposite the motion) acts for 2.0 s. Find the cart's velocity after each impulse.

question.html: Impulse Force Time acting First +12 N 1.5 s Second −15 N 2.0 s

body.html: 𝑚= 5.5 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= + 1.5 m/s. Find the velocity after the first impulse and after the second.
Impulse = 𝐹𝛥𝑡 (the area under the 𝐹–𝑡 graph) = 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝑝<sub>𝑖</sub>= 𝑚𝛥𝑣. The impulses are applied one after the other.
First impulse: 𝐽<sub>1</sub> = ( + 12 N)(1.5 s) = + 18 N · s.
Second impulse: 𝐽<sub>2</sub> = ( −15 N)(2.0 s) = −30 N · s.

answer.html: After the first impulse: 4.8 m/s in the original direction. After the second: 0.68 m/s in the opposite direction (the cart has reversed).

check.html: The second impulse is bigger than the first, so the net impulse is −12 N · s and the cart ends with 1.5 −12 / 5.5 = −0.68 m/s.

items.title: 4 (Lesson 1 Practice): A 310.0-kg jet ski speeds up from 4.00 m/s to 19.0 m/s in 45.0 s. (a) Sketch the situation. (b) Find the change in momentum and the impulse. (c) Find the average force on the jet ski.

body.html: 𝑚= 310.0 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= 4.00 m/s, 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>= 19.0 m/s, 𝛥𝑡= 45.0 s.
𝐹𝛥𝑡= 𝛥𝑝= 𝑚(𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>).

Sketch: "before" jet ski with a short arrow labeled 4.00 m/s; "after" the same jet ski with a long arrow labeled 19.0 m/s, both pointing in +x. 𝛥𝑝= 𝑚(𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>) = (310.0 kg)(19.0 −4.00) m/s = 4.65 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg · m/s The impulse equals 𝛥𝑝.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑝= 4.65 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg · m/s forward; impulse = 4.65 × 10<sup>3</sup> N · s forward.
103 N (forward).

check.html: A modest force over a long time makes a large impulse; N·s = kg·m/s.

items.title: 5 (Lesson 1 Practice, Challenge, parts a–b): A 75.0-kg passenger rides in a car that hits a barrier at 22 m/s and is stopped in 0.15 s. (a) What average force acts on the passenger? (b) What mass has a weight equal to that force? Could you hold yourself back with your arms?

body.html: 𝑚= 75.0 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= + 22 m/s, 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>= 0, 𝛥𝑡= 0.15 s. Find 𝐹, then the mass whose weight equals 𝐹.
Impulse-momentum theorem, then 𝑊= 𝑚𝑔.
Sketch: a passenger in a car moving right at 22 m/s toward a barrier; after, the passenger at rest; an arrow for the force pointing left. (a)
(b) The mass whose weight is 1.1 × 10<sup>4</sup> N:

answer.html: 1.1 × 10<sup>4</sup> N directed backward (opposite the motion; −1.1 × 10<sup>4</sup> N with the car's direction positive).
About 1.1 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg, the mass of a small car. No: you cannot hold up 1100 kg, so your arms cannot stop your body in a crash.

check.html: The force is about 15 times the passenger's weight (735 N), which is typical for a hard crash.

body.html: 𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>= 3.2 × 10<sup>3</sup> rev/min, 𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub>= 0, 𝐼= 5.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> kg · m<sup>2</sup>, |𝜏| = 0.15 N · m. Find 𝛥𝑡.
Angular impulse-angular momentum theorem: 𝜏𝛥𝑡= 𝐿<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝐿<sub>𝑖</sub>= −𝐼𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>.
Convert: 𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>= 3.2 × 10<sup>3</sup>

answer.html: About 12 s.

check.html: A small bearing torque acting on a spinning wheel takes several seconds to stop it, as expected.

items.title: the spin 𝜔 in rad/s and the average torque.

body.html: 𝜔= 5.4 × 10<sup>2</sup> rpm, 𝐼= 1.2 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> kg · m<sup>2</sup>, 𝛥𝑡= 0.20 s, starting from rest.
𝜏𝛥𝑡= 𝐼𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝐼𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub> with 𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>= 0.

items.title: 8 (Lesson 1 Practice): A flywheel in a toy engine spins at 3.5 rev/s and has a moment of inertia of 0.110 kg · m2. Find its angular velocity in rad/s and the angular impulse needed to bring it up to that speed from rest.

body.html: 𝑓= 3.5 rev/s, 𝐼= 0.110 kg · m<sup>2</sup>, 𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>= 0.
Angular impulse = 𝛥𝐿= 𝐼(𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>).

answer.html: 𝜔= 22 rad/s; angular impulse = 2.4 kg · m<sup>2</sup> / s (2.4 N · m · s).

check.html: kg·m²/s are the units of angular momentum, as expected.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 9 (Momentum): A freight train is parked at a station. A bumblebee flies past the platform at 3 m/s. Which has more momentum in the ground frame?

body.html: 𝑝= 𝑚𝑣. Momentum depends on velocity. The parked train has 𝑣= 0, so 𝑝= 0. The bee has a tiny mass but a nonzero speed.

answer.html: The flying bee has more momentum, because the parked train has zero velocity and therefore zero momentum.

check.html: Parked means 𝑣= 0, so 𝑝= 𝑚· 0 = 0 no matter how large the mass.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 10 (Direction): Two cyclists of equal mass ride at the same speed along a straight road, one traveling east and one traveling west. Do they have the same momentum? Draw their momentum vectors.

body.html: Momentum is a vector with the direction of the velocity. Take east as +x: traveling east, →𝑝= + 𝑚𝑣^𝑥; traveling west, →𝑝= −𝑚𝑣^𝑥. Draw two arrows of equal length pointing in opposite directions.

answer.html: No. The magnitudes are equal, but the directions are opposite, so the momentum vectors are opposite (+mv versus -mv).

check.html: Their vector sum is zero, and their difference is 2𝑚𝑣, not zero.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 11 (Catching): A goalkeeper catches a hard-kicked ball by letting her hands move backward with the ball as it arrives, instead of holding her hands stiff. Why does this hurt less?

body.html: The ball's momentum must go to zero (relative to her hands). The impulse 𝐹𝛥𝑡= 𝛥𝑝 needed is fixed by the ball's mass and speed. Moving her hands with the ball makes the stopping time 𝛥𝑡 longer.

answer.html: The impulse needed to stop the ball is fixed, so giving with the ball lengthens the stopping time and reduces the average force on her hands.

check.html: Stiff hands give a short 𝛥𝑡 and a large 𝐹, which stings or injures.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 12 (Tennis ball): A 0.0570-kg tennis ball arrives at a racket at 32.0 m/s and leaves in the opposite direction at 41.0 m/s. The contact time is 5.0 ms. (a) Draw the momentum before and after. (b) Find the change in momentum. (c) Find the impulse. (d) Find the average force on the ball.

body.html: 𝑚= 0.0570 kg. Take the ball's initial direction as positive: 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= + 32.0 m/s, 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>= −41.0 m/s, 𝛥𝑡= 5.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> s.
𝑝= 𝑚𝑣; impulse = 𝛥𝑝; 𝐹= impulse / 𝛥𝑡.
(a) Arrows: before, an arrow of length ∝1.82 pointing right ( + ); after, a longer arrow ( ∝2.34) pointing left ( −).
(c) Impulse = 𝛥𝑝= −4.16 N · s. (d)

answer.html: Momentum before: 1.82 kg·m/s toward the racket; after: 2.34 kg·m/s away from the racket (opposite direction, longer arrow).
𝛥𝑝= 4.16 kg · m/s, in the direction of the ball's final motion.
Impulse = 4.16 N · s, in the direction of the returning ball.
8.3 × 10<sup>2</sup> N (about 830 N), in the direction of the returning ball.

check.html: The force is large (over 1000 times the ball's weight) because the contact time is only a few milliseconds.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 13 (Wall bounce): A rubber ball is thrown horizontally at a wall and bounces straight back with the same speed it had before hitting. Are the change in momentum and the impulse zero? Describe the momentum arrows.

body.html: Same speed does not mean same momentum, because the velocity reverses. Take the direction toward the wall as +. Before: 𝑝<sub>𝑖</sub>= + 𝑚𝑣. After: 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>= −𝑚𝑣. 𝛥𝑝= 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝑝<sub>𝑖</sub>= −2𝑚𝑣.

answer.html: No, the change in momentum and the impulse are not zero; each has magnitude 2𝑚𝑣 and is directed away from the wall. Momentum arrows: an arrow toward the wall before, an equal-length arrow away from the wall after.

check.html: The wall must push the ball away from it during contact, which gives an impulse away from the wall.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 14 (Frame of reference): A passenger sits on a train moving at 30 m/s past a station. A coffee cup rests on her tray table. What is the momentum of the cup as seen by the passenger, and by a person standing on the platform?

body.html: Momentum 𝑝= 𝑚𝑣 depends on velocity, and velocity depends on the observer's frame.

answer.html: Relative to the passenger the cup is at rest, so its momentum is zero. Relative to the platform it moves at 30 m/s, so it has momentum 𝑚(30 m/s) in the train's direction. Because velocity is measured relative to a frame, so is momentum.

check.html: Different observers get different values of 𝑝 for the same object.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 15 (Ice dancer extends arms): A spinning ice dancer holds her arms tight against her body, then stretches both arms straight out to the sides. What happens to her spin rate, and why?

body.html: Angular momentum 𝐿= 𝐼𝜔 is conserved if no net external torque acts.

answer.html: No external torque acted on her (the ice and gravity gave essentially no torque). Stretching her arms out increased her moment of inertia 𝐼, so her angular velocity 𝜔 decreased to keep 𝐿= 𝐼𝜔 constant.

check.html: 𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub>/ 𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>= 𝐼<sub>𝑖</sub>/ 𝐼<sub>𝑓</sub>< 1 since 𝐼<sub>𝑓</sub>> 𝐼<sub>𝑖</sub>.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 16 (Pellets: stick vs. bounce): Two identical-mass pellets are fired at the same speed at a wooden block. A clay pellet sticks to the block. A rubber pellet bounces straight back. Which pellet delivers the larger impulse to the block? Explain with a momentum diagram.

body.html: Take the pellet's initial velocity as +𝑣 (toward the block). If it sticks, the pellet's final velocity is the block's tiny velocity, roughly 0, so 𝛥𝑝<sub>pellet</sub> ≈−𝑚𝑣. If it bounces back, 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>= −𝑚𝑣′ (with 𝑣′ > 0), so 𝛥𝑝<sub>pellet</sub> = −𝑚(𝑣+ 𝑣′). The bounce has the larger magnitude. The impulse on the block is equal and opposite to the pellet's, so it is larger for the rubber pellet. Diagram: initial arrow of length 𝑚𝑣 pointing toward the block; for "stick" almost no final arrow; for "bounce" a final arrow pointing back.

answer.html: The rubber pellet delivers the larger impulse to the block, because its momentum changes by more (𝑚(𝑣+ 𝑣′) versus about 𝑚𝑣).

check.html: Same logic as the wall bounce: reversing direction roughly doubles the change in momentum.

items.title: Unit 3, "Why is energy important to humans and society?" and Ask Questions (open- ended)

body.html: A prompt to write your own questions about the crash-test photo and add them to the class question board. There is no single numerical answer.
The photo shows a collision where a body is stopped quickly and an air bag acts on it. Good questions are about momentum, forces and energy in a collision.
Sample questions you could post: What is energy? How much force acts on a person in a crash? Why does an air bag reduce injury? Where does the energy of the moving car go in a crash?

answer.html: "What is energy?", "How does an air bag change the force on a passenger?", "Where does the car's kinetic energy go during a crash?"

check.html: Questions should be testable with measurements (mass, speed, time, force).

items.title: Module 9, CER: "How do rockets accelerate once they reach space?" (claim, evidence, reasoning)

body.html: Make a claim about how a rocket speeds up with nothing to push against, then support it.
A rocket plus its fuel is a closed, isolated system in space. The total momentum is constant, so when exhaust gas is thrown backward, the rocket must gain forward momentum (Newton's third law).

Claim: A rocket accelerates in space by expelling exhaust gas backward at high speed; the gas pushes the rocket forward. Evidence: Example Problem 4 and Problems 21–22: when one part of a system moves one way, the rest recoils the other way with equal and opposite momentum (𝑚<sub>rocket</sub>𝑣<sub>rocket</sub> = −𝑚<sub>gas</sub>𝑣<sub>gas</sub>). Skater push (Figure 11) shows the same thing. Reasoning: Initial momentum is zero (or constant) and no external force acts, so momentum is conserved. The gas gains backward momentum, so the rocket gains an equal forward momentum. No air or ground is needed.

answer.html: A rocket accelerates in space by recoil: ejecting gas backward gives the gas backward momentum, and conservation of momentum gives the rocket an equal forward momentum.

check.html: Matches Problem 21 (a 4.00-kg rocket expelling 50 g of gas at 625 m/s recoils at about 7.8 m/s).

items.title: Focus Question: How do air bags work to save lives?

body.html: The impulse needed to stop a person, 𝐹𝛥𝑡= 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝑝<sub>𝑖</sub>, is fixed by the change in momentum. An air bag lengthens 𝛥𝑡, so the force 𝐹 is smaller; it also spreads the force over a larger area.

answer.html: An air bag increases the stopping time, so the same impulse is delivered by a smaller average force spread over a larger area, reducing injury.

check.html: Same 𝛥𝑝, larger 𝛥𝑡 means smaller 𝐹 (see Problem 16 and Problem 5 for numbers).

items.title: Figure 1 prompt: "How can you calculate the change in velocity of the baseball?"

body.html: Find the impulse (area under the force-time graph), set it equal to 𝑚𝛥𝑣.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑣=<sub> </sub><sup>impulse</sup>
. The book carries this out in the text (already solved in book).

items.title: Figure 5, Analyze: How does extending her arms affect the diver's motion?

body.html: In the air no torque acts (ignoring air resistance), so 𝐿= 𝐼𝜔 stays constant. Extending the arms moves mass away from the axis, increasing 𝐼.
𝐼<sub>𝑖</sub>𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>= 𝐼<sub>𝑓</sub>𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub>, so 𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>(𝐼<sub>𝑖</sub>/ 𝐼<sub>𝑓</sub>). A larger 𝐼<sub>𝑓</sub> gives a smaller 𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub>.

answer.html: Extending her arms increases her moment of inertia, so she rotates more slowly (and she straightens out for a clean entry).

check.html: Opposite of tucking, which makes her spin faster.

items.title: Cause and Effect (Crosscutting Concepts, Figure 6): how skaters spin and how to test it

body.html: Pushing the skate into the ice makes the ice push back, giving a torque and so an angular impulse 𝜏𝛥𝑡= 𝛥𝐿 that starts the spin. Once spinning, 𝐿= 𝐼𝜔 is nearly constant, so changing 𝐼 changes 𝜔: arms/leg in means smaller 𝐼 and faster spin; arms/leg out means larger 𝐼 and slower spin. A second push with the free skate (opposing torque) stops the spin. Work (test plan): Have a skater (or a person on a rotating stool holding weights) start a spin, then change arm position. Record the spin rate by video (rotations per second) for arms out and arms in. Repeat with different weights. Compare 𝐼<sub>𝑖</sub>𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub> with 𝐼<sub>𝑓</sub>𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub> using estimated 𝐼.

answer.html: Torque from the ice starts or stops the spin (cause: push into ice; effect: angular impulse changes 𝐿). With no torque, pulling in arms lowers 𝐼 and raises 𝜔 so 𝐼𝜔 stays constant. Test by measuring spin rate with arms out versus in.

check.html: Measured 𝜔<sub>in</sub> / 𝜔<sub>out</sub> should equal 𝐼<sub>out</sub> / 𝐼<sub>in</sub>.

items.title: 1 (Lesson 1 Practice, parts a–b)

question.html: A 725-kg car moves at 115 km/h east. (a) Find its momentum and sketch it. (b) A 2175-kg car has the same momentum; what is its velocity?

body.html: 𝑚<sub>1</sub> = 725 kg, 𝑣<sub>1</sub> = 115 km/h = 31.9 m/s east; 𝑚<sup>2</sup> = 2175 kg, 𝑝<sub>2</sub> = 𝑝<sub>1</sub>. Find 𝑝<sub>1</sub> and 𝑣<sup>2</sup>.
Momentum is 𝑝= 𝑚𝑣 (a vector, same direction as the velocity).
Convert speed: 115 km/h ×<sub> </sub><sup>1000</sup><sup> </sup><sup>m</sup>
Sketch: a car drawn at the left with an arrow pointing east (to the right) above it labeled 𝑝<sub>1</sub>; the axis +x points east. For the heavier car, 𝑝<sub>2</sub> = 𝑝<sub>1</sub>, so

answer.html: 2.32 × 10<sup>4</sup> kg · m/s, east.
10.6 m/s (about 38 km/h), east.

check.html: The car is 3 times as massive, so its speed is one third (31.9/3 ≈ 10.6).

items.title: 2 (Lesson 1 Practice)

question.html: The 725-kg car brakes for 2.0 s with an average force of 5.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> N. (a) Impulse? (b) Final momentum and velocity?

body.html: 𝑚= 725 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= + 31.9 m/s (east positive), 𝛥𝑡= 2.0 s, 𝐹= −5.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> N (braking force points west). Find 𝐹𝛥𝑡, 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>, 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>.
Impulse-momentum theorem 𝐹𝛥𝑡= 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝑝<sub>𝑖</sub>.
Sketch: "before" car with arrow east labeled 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= 31.9 m/s, "after" car with a shorter arrow east labeled 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>= 18 m/s, and a west-pointing arrow for the impulse.

answer.html: change in momentum (impulse) = 1.0 × 10<sup>4</sup> kg · m/s (1.0 × 10<sup>4</sup> N · s), directed west.
𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>= 1.3 × 10<sup>4</sup> kg · m/s east; 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>= 18 m/s east (about 65 km/h).

check.html: The car slows but still moves east; 18 m/s is less than 31.9 m/s.

items.title: 3 (Lesson 1 Practice)

question.html: A 7.0-kg object moves at 2.0 m/s and receives two impulses in the direction of its motion (Figure 2). Find the speed and direction after each impulse.

body.html: Reading Figure 2: first graph, force = + 5 N from 𝑡= 1 s to 2 s (a rectangle above the axis). Second graph, force = −5 N from 1 s to 2 s (below the axis). 𝑚= 7.0 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= + 2.0 m/s.
Impulse = area under the 𝐹–𝑡 graph = 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝑝<sub>𝑖</sub>. The impulses are applied one after the other.
First impulse: area = ( + 5 N)(1 s) = + 5 N · s.
Second impulse: area = ( −5 N)(1 s) = −5 N · s.

answer.html: After the first impulse: 2.7 m/s in the original direction of motion. After the second: 2.0 m/s, still in the original direction (the impulses cancel).

check.html: The two impulses are equal and opposite, so the net change is zero and the object returns to its original speed.

items.title: 4 (Lesson 1 Practice)

question.html: A 240.0-kg snowmobile speeds up from 6.00 m/s to 28.0 m/s in 60.0 s. (a) Sketch. (b) Change in momentum and impulse. (c) Average force.

body.html: 𝑚= 240.0 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= 6.00 m/s, 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>= 28.0 m/s, 𝛥𝑡= 60.0 s.
𝐹𝛥𝑡= 𝛥𝑝= 𝑚(𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>).

Sketch: "before" snowmobile with a short arrow labeled 6.00 m/s; "after" the same snowmobile with a long arrow labeled 28.0 m/s, both pointing in +x. 𝛥𝑝= 𝑚(𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>) = (240.0 kg)(28.0 −6.00) m/s = 5.28 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg · m/s The impulse equals 𝛥𝑝.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑝= 5.28 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg · m/s forward; impulse = 5.28 × 10<sup>3</sup> N · s forward.
88.0 N (forward).

check.html: A modest force acting for a long time gives a large impulse; units N·s = kg·m/s.

items.title: 5 (Lesson 1 Practice)

question.html: A 60.0-kg person is in the car that hits the wall in Example Problem 1 (speed 26 m/s, stopped in 0.20 s).

body.html: 𝑚= 60.0 kg, 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= + 26 m/s, 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>= 0, 𝛥𝑡= 0.20 s. Find 𝐹, then the mass whose weight equals 𝐹.
Impulse-momentum theorem, then 𝑊= 𝑚𝑔.
Sketch: a person in a car moving right at 26 m/s toward a wall; after, the person at rest; an arrow for the force pointing left. (a)
(b) Mass with weight 7.8 × 10<sup>3</sup> N:

answer.html: 7.8 × 10<sup>3</sup> N directed backward (opposite the motion; −7.8 × 10<sup>3</sup> N with the car's direction positive).
About 8.0 × 10<sup>2</sup> kg (about the mass of a small car). No: you cannot lift 800 kg, so your arms cannot stop your body in a crash.

check.html: The force is about 13 times the person's weight, which is typical for a hard crash.

items.title: 6 (Lesson 1 Practice)

question.html: A saw blade (𝐼= 8.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> kg · m<sup>2</sup>) spins at 5.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> rpm; friction gives an average torque of 2.3 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup> N · m. How long to stop?

body.html: 𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>= 5.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> rev/min, 𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub>= 0, 𝐼= 8.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> kg · m<sup>2</sup>, |𝜏| = 0.23 N · m. Find 𝛥𝑡.
Angular impulse-angular momentum theorem: 𝜏𝛥𝑡= 𝐿<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝐿<sub>𝑖</sub>= −𝐼𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>.
Convert: 𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>= 5.0 × 10<sup>3</sup>

answer.html: About 18 s.

check.html: "Several seconds" matches the problem statement.

items.title: 7 (Lesson 1 Practice)

question.html: A curve ball spins at 6.0 × 10<sup>2</sup> rpm, 𝐼= 8.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> kg · m<sup>2</sup>, pitcher's motion lasts 0.15 s. Find 𝜔 and the average torque.

body.html: 𝜔= 6.0 × 10<sup>2</sup> rpm, 𝐼= 8.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> kg · m<sup>2</sup>, 𝛥𝑡= 0.15 s, starting from rest.
𝜏𝛥𝑡= 𝐼𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝐼𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub> with 𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>= 0.

answer.html: 𝜔= 63 rad/s; average torque = 3.4 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>2</sup> N · m.

check.html: A small torque makes sense for a light ball with a tiny moment of inertia.

items.title: 8 (Lesson 1 Practice)

question.html: The wheel spins at 5.0 rev/s with 𝐼= 0.060 kg · m<sup>2</sup>. Find 𝜔 and the angular impulse given to it (starting from rest).

body.html: Angular impulse = 𝛥𝐿= 𝐼(𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>).

answer.html: 𝜔= 31 rad/s; angular impulse = 1.9 kg · m<sup>2</sup> / s (1.9 N · m · s).

check.html: Units kg·m²/s are the units of angular momentum, as expected.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 9 (Momentum: truck vs. raindrop)

body.html: 𝑝= 𝑚𝑣. Momentum depends on velocity; the truck is at rest in the ground frame, so 𝑣= 0 and 𝑝= 0. The raindrop has a tiny mass but nonzero speed.

answer.html: The falling raindrop has more momentum, because the parked truck has zero velocity and therefore zero momentum.

check.html: Parked means 𝑣= 0, so 𝑝= 𝑚· 0 = 0 no matter how big the mass.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 10 (south vs. north)

body.html: Momentum is a vector with the direction of the velocity. Take north as +y: traveling north, →𝑝= + 𝑚𝑣^𝑦; traveling south, →𝑝= −𝑚𝑣^𝑦. Draw the two arrows of equal length pointing in opposite directions.

answer.html: Yes, they differ. The magnitudes are equal, but the directions are opposite, so the momentum vectors are opposite (+mv versus -mv).

check.html: Their vector difference is 2𝑚𝑣, not zero.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 11 (bending the knees)

body.html: Your momentum just before landing goes to zero. The impulse 𝐹𝛥𝑡= 𝛥𝑝 is fixed by your landing speed and mass. Bending the knees makes the stopping time 𝛥𝑡 longer.

answer.html: The impulse needed to stop you is fixed, so bending your knees lengthens the stopping time and reduces the average force on your legs and bones.

check.html: Landing stiff-legged has a short 𝛥𝑡 and a large 𝐹, which can injure you.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 12 (softball)

question.html: A 0.174-kg softball arrives at 26.0 m/s and leaves in the opposite direction at 38.0 m/s. Contact time 0.80 ms.

body.html: 𝑚= 0.174 kg. Take the ball's initial direction as positive: 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= + 26.0 m/s, 𝑣<sub>𝑓</sub>= −38.0 m/s, 𝛥𝑡= 0.80 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> s.
𝑝= 𝑚𝑣; impulse = 𝛥𝑝; 𝐹= impulse / 𝛥𝑡.
(a) Arrows: before, an arrow of length ∝4.52 pointing right ( + ); after, a longer arrow ( ∝6.61) pointing left ( −).
(c) Impulse = 𝛥𝑝= −11.1 N · s. (d)

answer.html: Momentum before: 4.52 kg·m/s toward the bat; after: 6.61 kg·m/s away from the bat (opposite direction, longer arrow).
𝛥𝑝= 11.1 kg · m/s, in the direction of the ball's final motion (opposite to its original motion).
Impulse = 11.1 N · s, in the direction of the batted ball.
1.4 × 10<sup>4</sup> N (about 14,000 N), in the direction of the batted ball.

check.html: Force is very large because the contact time is under a millisecond; compare the baseball example in the text.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 13 (bouncing basketball)

body.html: Same speed does not mean same momentum, because the velocity reverses. Take up as +. Before: 𝑝<sub>𝑖</sub>= −𝑚𝑣 (moving down). After: 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>= + 𝑚𝑣 (moving up). 𝛥𝑝= 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>−𝑝<sub>𝑖</sub>= + 2𝑚𝑣.

answer.html: No, the change in momentum and the impulse are not zero; each equals 2𝑚𝑣 directed upward (away from the floor). Momentum arrows: a downward arrow before, an equal-length upward arrow after.

check.html: The floor must push up on the ball during contact, which gives an upward impulse.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 14 (frame of reference)

body.html: Momentum 𝑝= 𝑚𝑣 depends on velocity, and velocity depends on the observer's frame.

answer.html: Because velocity is measured relative to a frame, so is momentum. A car moving at 25 m/s has momentum in the ground frame but zero momentum as seen by its driver (who moves with it).

check.html: Different observers get different values of 𝑝 for the same object.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 15 (skater pulls in his arms)

body.html: Angular momentum 𝐿= 𝐼𝜔 is conserved if no net external torque acts.

answer.html: No external torque acted on him (the ice and gravity gave essentially no torque). Pulling his arms in decreased his moment of inertia 𝐼, so his angular velocity 𝜔 increased to keep 𝐿= 𝐼𝜔 constant.

check.html: 𝜔<sub>𝑓</sub>/ 𝜔<sub>𝑖</sub>= 𝐼<sub>𝑖</sub>/ 𝐼<sub>𝑓</sub>> 1 since 𝐼<sub>𝑓</sub>< 𝐼<sub>𝑖</sub>.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 16 (archer: stick vs. bounce)

body.html: Take the arrow's initial velocity as +𝑣 (toward target). If the arrow sticks: 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>= 0, so 𝛥𝑝<sub>arrow</sub> = −𝑚𝑣. If it bounces back: 𝑝<sub>𝑓</sub>= −𝑚𝑣′ (with 𝑣′ > 0), so 𝛥𝑝<sub>arrow</sub> = −𝑚(𝑣+ 𝑣′). The arrow's change in momentum is larger in magnitude in the bounce case. The impulse on the target is equal and opposite to the arrow's, so it is larger for the bouncing arrow. Diagram: initial arrow of length 𝑚𝑣 pointing toward the target; for "stick" no final arrow; for "bounce" a final arrow pointing back.

answer.html: The arrows that bounce off produce a bigger impulse on the target, because their momentum changes by more (𝑚(𝑣+ 𝑣′) versus 𝑚𝑣).

check.html: The same logic as the basketball: reversing direction doubles the change in momentum.
